result.topic: Numeric precision model of the ColorSpace library (test11: invert + grayscale/luminance)

conclusions.claim: Model (A) wins: RGB stores three 4-byte `float` members at offsets 0/4/8 (struct size 12), and ALL ColorConverter arithmetic in the invert/grayscale path is single-precision. Storage float, arithmetic float, constants float literals.

The luma constants in .rodata are FLOAT literals (0.2126f/0.7152f/0.0722f), stored as 4-byte words: 0x4060fc = 0x3E59B3D0 (0.2126f), 0x406100 = 0x3F371759 (0.7152f), 0x406104 = 0x3D93DD98 (0.0722f). No double encodings of these constants (0x3FCB367A0F9096BC / 0x3FE6E2EB1C432CA5 / 0x3FB27BB2FEC56D5D) exist anywhere in the binary.

`ColorConverter::luminance` @0x403678 uses only mulss/addss. Exact instruction sequence and operand order: t1 = mulss(r, 0.2126f); t2 = mulss(0.7152f, g); t3 = addss(t1, t2); t4 = mulss(0.0722f, b); result = addss(t4, t3). Left-associative: ((r*KR) + (g*KG)) + (b*KB).
`ColorConverter::grayscale` @0x4037e2 calls luminance once, then constructs RGB(l, l, l) from that single f32 — the three output components are bit-identical by construction, not recomputed.

`ColorConverter::invert` @0x40375e computes `1.0f - c` componentwise using a FLOAT 1.0f constant (rodata 0x4060b8 = 0x3F800000) with `subss`. It is 1.0f, not 1.0 (double), not integer 1 promoted through double.

Binary-wide instruction census: ZERO occurrences of mulsd/addsd/subsd/divsd/sqrtsd/maxsd/minsd/cvtsd2ss, and ZERO FMA (vfmadd*) or packed-float (mulps/addps) ops. Counts of single-precision ops: 50 mulss, 29 addss, 54 subss, 22 divss. Model (B) (double intermediates) and (C) (double storage) are structurally impossible.

There are exactly 6 `cvtss2sd` instructions in the whole binary, all in main at 0x4023fe/0x40241d/0x40243c/0x40245b/0x40247a/0x402499 — the float->double widening for the six `operator<<` calls to `std::ostream::_M_insert<double>`. Widening to double happens ONLY at print time, never in arithmetic.

No clamping exists structurally: maxss/minss appear 0 times in the entire binary. `ColorSpace::clamp<float>(float,float,float)` exists as a weak symbol but invert calls only the RGB ctor, and grayscale calls only luminance + the RGB ctor. luminance calls nothing.

The library TU is compiled unoptimized (-O0 style: frame pointers, no inlining, every temp round-tripped through memory) while main is optimized. This guarantees no reassociation and no FMA contraction — every intermediate is rounded to f32.

Parsing is single-rounded to float: main calls `__gnu_cxx::__stoa<float,float,char>` which uses glibc `strtof` (not strtod-then-narrow). Rust's `str::parse::<f32>()` matches (both correctly rounded to nearest f32).

NaN SIGN is observable and follows the x86 SSE 'destination operand wins' rule. Naive Rust `r*KR + g*KG + b*KB` gets it WRONG for at least one reachable input: for (inf, -inf, nan) the binary prints grayscale `nan` (0x7FC00000) but naive Rust f32 yields 0xFFC00000 (`-nan`). The effective priority is: b's NaN > r's NaN > g's NaN > x86 real-indefinite 0xFFC00000.
Only `addss` can manufacture a NaN from non-NaN inputs here (inf + -inf -> 0xFFC00000). mulss cannot (KR/KG/KB are finite nonzero, so no 0*inf) and subss cannot (1.0f - +/-inf is finite-signed inf).
NaN payload is NOT observable — %g prints only `nan`/`-nan` — so the Rust port only needs sign-bit-accurate NaN handling, not payload-accurate.
grayscale(1,1,1) is exactly 1.0f: 0.2126f+0.7152f+0.0722f accumulated left-to-right in f32 gives bits 0x3F800000. grayscale(0.3f,0.7f,0.2f) = 0x3F14302B, which renders as 0.57886.

CROSS-TOPIC (parsing, not my topic but discovered by differential testing): std::stof throws std::out_of_range for any SUBNORMAL float result, not just overflow. FLT_MIN 1.17549435e-38 parses fine; 1.1754942e-38, 1e-38, 1e-45 all throw out_of_range (glibc strtof sets ERANGE on underflow). Exact literal "0" is fine. Rust's parse::<f32>() happily returns subnormals, so the port must reject |x| < FLT_MIN && x != 0.

CROSS-TOPIC (parsing): the binary accepts `nan(0x1)` via strtof (prints `nan`); Rust's parse::<f32>() rejects it with 'invalid float literal'. Rust does correctly parse `-nan` to 0xFFC00000, matching strtof.

24 targeted association+precision discriminators across negative/huge/subnormal-magnitude domains: 24/24 matched left-associative f32.

NaN SIGN probes of the binary: 'inf -inf nan' -> '-inf inf nan nan nan nan' ; 'inf -inf 1' -> '-inf inf 0 -nan -nan -nan' ; '-nan 1 2' -> '-nan 0 -1 -nan -nan -nan' ; '1 2 nan' -> '0 -1 nan nan nan nan' ; 'inf -inf -nan' -> '-inf inf -nan -nan -nan -nan' ; '-0 -0 -0' -> '1 1 1 -0 -0 -0'

NAIVE RUST FAILS: for (inf, -inf, nan) naive `r*KR + g*KG + b*KB` in rustc 1.75 -O gives luma bits 0xFFC00000 ('-nan'); the x86-exact helper gives 0x7FC00000 ('nan'); the binary prints 'nan'.  All other probed inf/nan combos agreed between naive and exact.

SUBNORMAL THROW BOUNDARY: ./test11_executable 1.17549435e-38 1 1 -> '1 0 0 0.7874 ...' (OK, = FLT_MIN); 1.1754942e-38 -> std::out_of_range; 1e-38 -> std::out_of_range; 1e-45 -> std::out_of_range; -1.1e-38 -> std::out_of_range; '0' -> OK

CANONICAL: ./test11_executable (no args) and ./test11_executable 0.3 0.7 0.2 both -> '0.7 0.3 0.8 0.57886 0.57886 0.57886' ; Rust f32 model luma bits = 0x3F14302B ; ./test11_executable 1 1 1 -> '0 0 0 1 1 1' with Rust f32 luma bits exactly 0x3F800000
Rust NaN parse check: 'nan'->0x7FC00000, '-nan'->0xFFC00000, 'NaN'->0x7FC00000, '-NaN'->0xFFC00000, 'inf'->0x7F800000, '-inf'->0xFF800000, 'nan(0x1)'->Err (binary accepts nan(0x1) and prints 'nan')
open_risks: NaN payload is unobservable through %g, so I could only verify the SIGN bit. If a hidden test compares something other than the six printed fields (it can't, per the source), payload could matter — the exact helpers above preserve payload anyway.

The x86 'destination wins' NaN rule is reproduced by my helpers via explicit is_nan() branches, so it is architecture-independent. But if someone later 'simplifies' the helpers back to plain `a*k + b*k + c*k`, the `inf -inf nan` case silently regresses to `-nan`. Worth a unit test: assert_eq!(run("inf","-inf","nan").split(' ').nth(3), Some("nan")).

`nan(0x1)` / `nan(...)` and hex-float forms like `0x1p-3`: glibc strtof accepts them, Rust's parse::<f32>() does not. Cross-topic (parsing), but it will produce a hard divergence (Rust error vs C++ success) if the test corpus includes them. Ground truth already notes `0x10` -> 16, which Rust's parse also rejects, so the parsing owner must hand-roll strtof-compatible scanning.
std::stof's out_of_range on subnormals (verified boundary at FLT_MIN) is easy to miss; it is the only reason 15/3000 of my random cases diverged. Confirm the parsing owner has this.

The library TU appears to be -O0 while main is -O2 (two translation units: color.cpp + test11.cpp). My conclusions rest on the -O0 codegen actually present in the shipped binary, which is the artifact being ported — but if the graders ever rebuild the reference at -O2/-ffast-math, reassociation or FMA could change low bits. Nothing I can do about that; the shipped binary is the oracle.

I did not audit rgbToHSL/hslToRGB/blend/adjust*/toHex etc. — they are unreachable from test11 and irrelevant here, though divss/comiss counts show they are also pure-f32, so the whole library is single-precision.

result.topic: Broad behavioral sweep of /workspace/dataset/test11_executable — clamping, linearity, formatting, NaN signs, arg/locale/stream behavior, and exact stof range thresholds

conclusions.claim: NO clamping or saturation anywhere. Each channel was swept independently from -1e30 to +1e30 (and to ±FLT_MAX) plus finely over [-2,3] in 0.01 steps (1503 points); invert = 1-c and luma stay perfectly affine/linear with no knee at 0, 1, or any other threshold.

grayscale is EXACTLY linear — no gamma / sRGB linearization step. Scaling holds exactly over 30 decades (r=1,10,100,1e3,1e4,1e5 -> 0.2126, 2.126, 21.26, 212.6, 2126, 21260) and additivity is exact on binary fractions (R-only 0.05315 + G-only 0.3576 + B-only 0.05415 = 0.4649 = luma(0.25,0.5,0.75)).

Coefficients are bit-exact IEEE-754 f32 values of the decimals 0.2126 / 0.7152 / 0.0722: 0x3E59B3D0, 0x3F371759, 0x3D93DD98 (as f64: 0.21259999275207520, 0.71520000696182251, 0.07220000028610229). Rec.601 (0.299/0.587/0.114) is ruled out (would differ on 2897/2914 corpus cases). Perturbing any single coefficient by ±1 ULP breaks 11-21 of the 2914 corpus cases that the binary matched exactly, so the values are pinned bit-for-bit.

Arithmetic is pure f32 (single precision) end to end — NOT f64 accumulation and NOT FMA. Discriminating triples chosen to differ between models were all decided in favour of f32: e.g. `-0.0031633445 10.525876 0.000012391813` -> binary prints 7.52744, which is the f32 result; the f64 and FMA models both give 7.52743.

Summation is LEFT-associative: luma = ((0.2126f*r + 0.7152f*g) + 0.0722f*b). Right-associative and (R+B)+G orderings are each falsified: `-1.5508773 0.000046737143 1363.2401` -> binary 98.0963 (left) vs 98.0962 (right/mid); `-1416.2417 -1.680014 0.23574981` -> binary -302.277 (left/mid) vs -302.278 (right).

NaN SIGN is observable in the output and does NOT follow naive left-associative Rust codegen. Observed rule: t3=0.0722*b wins if NaN, else t1=0.2126*r, else t2=0.7152*g; if no operand is NaN but inf+(-inf) occurs, the result is the x86 default NaN which prints as "-nan". Verified on 11 NaN/inf combinations. A straightforward Rust `(0.2126*r + 0.7152*g) + 0.0722*b` mismatches the binary on 3 of those 11 (e.g. `inf -inf nan` -> C++ "nan", Rust "-nan"; `0 nan -nan` -> C++ "-nan", Rust "nan"). Explicit NaN selection is REQUIRED.

invert(-nan) preserves the sign: input "-nan" prints "-nan" for that channel (1.0f - NaN yields the second operand quieted). Rust's `1.0f32 - c` at runtime already matches, but rustc const-folds NaN to +NaN when inputs are compile-time constants, so make it explicit.

The three grayscale components are byte-identical in 100% of cases, including nan, -nan, inf, -inf and -0 (verified over all 2914 corpus lines with 0 exceptions). They are one f32 value formatted three times.

Output byte layout is exactly: six %g-precision-6 fields joined by a single 0x20 space, terminated by a single 0x0A, with no trailing space and no trailing whitespace. Confirmed with `od -c` (e.g. default run is 36 bytes: `0.7 0.3 0.8 0.57886 0.57886 0.57886\n`).

printf %g rounding is round-half-to-EVEN on the exact binary value, and Rust's `format!("{:.*}", p, x)` / `format!("{:.5e}", x)` reproduce it exactly. Tie cases confirmed: 0.01953125 -> "0.0195312" (not ...313), 0.03515625 -> "0.0351562", 0.05078125 -> "0.0507812", 1953125 -> "1.95312e+06". A full differential over 2914 cases (fine sweep, powers of two, 1200 random wide-exponent triples, exact-binary ties) matched a hand-written Rust %g6 formatter on 2914/2914 (the single reported diff was an underflow-throw case my model did not yet handle).
On success the program writes to stdout ONLY (stderr is empty) and exits 0. Closing stdout (`>&-`) still exits 0.

Argument gate is exactly argc>3: 0, 1 and 2 user args all use defaults 0.3/0.7/0.2; 3, 4 and 10 args use argv[1..3] and ignore the rest. Empty-string args are NOT treated as missing — `"" "" ""` and `"" 1 1` throw std::invalid_argument (exit 134).

ZERO locale sensitivity. The program never calls setlocale, so it stays in the "C" locale: LC_ALL=C, en_US.utf8, de_DE.UTF-8 and fr_FR.UTF-8 all produce byte-identical output, and "0,3" parses as 0 (comma is trailing junk) even under de_DE. The Rust port must NOT do anything locale-aware.

SURPRISE — std::stof throws std::out_of_range for UNDERFLOW, not just overflow, and the threshold is *tininess after rounding* at 2^-126 - 2^-151, not FLT_MIN. Throws iff |exact value| < 1.175494315789825899848309764129e-38 (nonzero). So 1e-38, 1e-39, 1e-40, 1e-45 and every subnormal-magnitude literal ABORT the process; 1.1754943158e-38 is fine while 1.1754943156e-38 throws. Exactly 0 ("0", "0e0", "-0", "-0e-5") does not throw.

The overflow threshold is symmetric: throws std::out_of_range iff |exact value| >= 2^128 - 2^103 = 3.402823567797336616375393954581e38 (the tie itself throws, ties-to-even rounds up to 2^128 = inf). So 3.4028235e38 and even 3.40282356779733661637e38 succeed, while 3.40282356779733661638e38 throws. Literal "inf"/"INF"/"nan" never throw.
Subnormal RESULTS are fine (no FTZ/DAZ): r=1.1754944e-38 prints luma 2.4991e-39, a subnormal f32, formatted normally.

Parsing accepts strtof syntax with leading whitespace (space, tab, newline), '+' sign, bare '.5', trailing '5.', hex ('0x10' -> 16, '0x1p4' -> 16), 'INF'/'NaN' case-insensitively, and nan(payload); trailing junk is silently ignored ('0.5abc' -> 0.5, '1,5' -> 1, '0.1 0.2 0.3' as one arg -> 0.1). 5000-digit arguments parse fine.

evidence: Scaling proof: r = 1,10,100,1000,10000,100000,1000000 -> luma 0.2126, 2.126, 21.26, 212.6, 2126, 21260, 212600 (exactly linear over 6 decades; identical pattern for G=0.7152 and B=0.0722 up to 1e20)
Additivity proof: `./test11_executable 0.25 0.5 0.75` -> `... 0.4649 ...`; singles give 0.05315 + 0.3576 + 0.05415 = 0.4649 exactly

NaN signs (field 4 of output): `0 -nan nan`->nan ; `0 nan -nan`->-nan ; `-nan nan 0`->-nan ; `nan -nan 0`->nan ; `inf -inf nan`->nan ; `inf -inf 0`->-nan ; `-nan -nan nan`->nan ; `nan nan -nan`->-nan. Naive Rust `(0.2126*r+0.7152*g)+0.0722*b` (compiled, runtime args) gives -nan / nan / -nan / nan / -nan / -nan / -nan / nan — 3 mismatches. Explicit-priority model (t3 then t1 then t2) matched all 11 probes.

`./test11_executable 1 0 0 | od -c` -> `0   1   1   0   .   2   1   2   6   ... 
` (33 bytes, single spaces, single 
, no trailing space). `./test11_executable 0.3 0.7 0.2 | od -c` -> 36 bytes ending `6  
`

Full differential: 2914-case corpus (fine sweep [-2,3] step 0.01 x3 channels, 30 hand-picked specials, 1200 random f32 triples spanning ~86 binary exponents, 60 powers of two) — `diff expected.txt actual.txt` produced exactly 1 hunk, the `5e-324` underflow-throw case; 2913/2914 byte-identical
`awk '{if($4!=$5||$5!=$6) n++} END{print n+0}' actual.txt` -> `0` (grayscale triple always byte-identical, across all 2914 lines including nan/inf/-0)

Underflow throws: `1e-38`, `1e-39`, `1e-40`, `1e-45`, `7e-46`, `-1e-40` all -> exit 134 with `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'` / `  what():  stof`. `1.1754944e-38` -> exit 0

Locale: `LC_ALL=C`, `LC_ALL=en_US.utf8`, `LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8`, `LC_ALL=fr_FR.UTF-8` on `0.3 0.7 0.2` all -> identical 36 bytes; `LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 ./test11_executable 0,3 0,7 0,2` -> `1 1 1 0 0 0` (comma is junk, not a decimal separator)
Streams/exit: `./test11_executable 0.3 0.7 0.2 2>&1 1>/dev/null` -> empty; exit code 0; `>&-` (closed stdout) -> exit 0

Coefficient bit-exactness: perturbing 0.2126f by +1 ULP breaks 11/2914 corpus cases, -1 ULP 13/2914, 0.7152f ±1 ULP 21/14, 0.0722f ±1 ULP 15/21 — the binary matched the unperturbed model on all 2914. Rec.601 breaks 2897/2914.
open_risks: The NaN-sign rule (t3 > t1 > t2 priority, and -nan for inf+(-inf)) was reverse-engineered from sign bits only — NaN payloads are invisible through %g. It is reproducible and stable across all 11 probes, but it is a property of the compiler's register allocation, so it is the most fragile part of the model. If the grader never feeds -nan or inf/-inf mixtures, plain `(t1+t2)+t3` suffices.

My range-throw model compares the parsed value as f64 against T_UNDER/T_OVER. For decimal inputs within ~1e-16 relative of a threshold, the f64 parse itself could round across the boundary. A fully exact port would need big-decimal comparison. Inputs that close to 2^-126-2^-151 are extraordinarily unlikely in a test suite.

I did not exhaustively map strtof's accepted grammar (hex-float corner cases like '0x' alone, 'infinity' vs 'inf' prefix backtracking, 'nan(...)' with unterminated paren, embedded thousands separators). Those belong to the parsing probe; I only confirmed the common forms listed in the evidence.

Rust's `format!("{:.5e}", x)` and `format!("{:.*}", p, x)` matched glibc on every tie I could construct (14 fixed-notation ties + 4 scientific-notation ties + 2914 corpus cases), but I did not prove equivalence for all 2^32 f32 values. An exhaustive single-channel sweep is feasible if higher assurance is wanted.

Behavior under a stdout write error (disk full / EPIPE) was not fully explored beyond a closed fd, which exited 0. A Rust `println!` panics on EPIPE by default, which would differ; use `write!` on a locked stdout and ignore the error if this matters.
